title: Absolute power divided into first (the natural faculty) and second (habits)
source_text: XXXI. Rursus potentia ista absoluta ab eo distinguitur in primam & secundam. Prima ab ipso vocatur ipsa naturalis facultas, per quam homo capax est bene & male agendi, quod brutis non convenit. Potentia absoluta bene agendi quam secundam vocat, consistit in habitibus potentiam naturalem ad bene agendum determinantibus, sive inclinantibus.
pass_a_gloss: XXXI. Again that absolute power is distinguished by him into first and second. The first is called by him the natural faculty itself, by which man is capable of acting well and ill, which does not belong to brutes. The absolute power of acting well which he calls second, consists in habits determining, or inclining, the natural power to acting well.
pass_b_english: He divides this absolute power further into a first and a second. The first is simply the natural faculty that makes man able to act well or badly, something beasts do not have. The second absolute power of acting well consists in habits that determine or incline the natural power toward acting well.

lemmas.gloss: which does not belong to brutes

lemmas.latin: consistit in habitibus potentiam naturalem ad bene agendum determinantibus
lemmas.gloss: consists in habits determining the natural power to acting well

choices.why: The Schools' distinction between a remote (merely capable) and a proximate (ready to act) power; kept as technical terms.
